title: Climate-only daily LSTMs explained 40-45% of the post-1997 runoff deficit in 175 south-east Australian catchments; the rest was a gradual mainland decline but a 1997 step in Tasmania and SW WA
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff fell 12-25% below its 1951-1996 relation to rain. Fixed-form climate models explained at most one third. What part can a flexible model that sees only climate produce? Approach: a regional LSTM on daily CAMELS-AUS v2.03 data of 561 catchments (rain, evaporative demand, temperature, vapour pressure, radiation, vapour-pressure deficit, 1- and 3-year rain). Four leave-window-out folds inside 1951-1996; models trained on 1951-1996 predict 1997-2021. Reference: a per-catchment linear annual model with the same folds. Target: 175 SE-AU catchments. Plan written before any prediction was inspected. Results: the LSTM removed 45% (95% CI 14-71%) of the 2010-2021 linear deficit (-10.7% against -19.6% of mean runoff) and 40% (24-56%) in 1997-2009: 'partial' by the planned rule. Both post-1997 departures were below all four cross-validated pre-1997 windows (+26%, +9%, +3.5%, -2%). The LSTM removed 84% of the 1983-1996 low, so the earlier lows were mostly climatic. It removed 32-38% in Victoria and 62-74% in NSW+ACT. It produced part of the loss of rain sensitivity: slope ratio 0.90 against 0.75 observed in 2010-2021. An LSTM trained on all years 1951-2021 still left a contrast between the eras. Post hoc: climate-adjusted mainland departures fitted a gradual decline of -3.5% per decade from 1959 (CI -5.6 to -1.9); a 1997 step added -2% (-8.5 to +4.1). Tasmania and south-west WA had 1997 steps of -19% and -25%, with best break year 1997 in a 1975-2012 scan. The northern summer-rain control had no deficit and no trend. Conclusion: climate dynamics explain more of the deficit than fixed models showed and explain the earlier lows, but 55-60% remains. It is a slow mainland decline since the 1950s plus a 1997 step in southern winter-rain regions, not one drought-induced state shift. Limitations: one LSTM architecture and few seeds; possible time-proxy use of temperature; 730-day memory; gridded rain inhomogeneity; regional tests are post hoc.

citations.reason: We use its 175-catchment set and departure definition. Our flexible climate model shows that its earlier lows (1959-1971, 1983-1995) are mostly climatic, which supports its conclusion that the post-1997 deficit is not a repeat of them.
We reproduce its post-1997 deficit and loss of rain sensitivity out of sample; a climate-only LSTM reproduces only part of the sensitivity loss.

It found that daily climate explains at most about one third of multidecadal efficiency changes. A flexible LSTM explains 40-45% of the post-1997 deficit and most of the 1983-1996 low, so fixed-form models understate the climatic part.
Its GR4J storage test explained 16% of the post-2009 loss; we test a model class without a fixed store structure.
After climate adjustment, NSW+ACT efficiency declined gradually (best break 1979), as it found; for Victoria a 1990s step and a trend fit about equally well.
Our climate-adjusted mainland series also shows a gradual decline from before 1981 rather than a 1997 step.
It linked the 1997 step to winter-rain share; we find 1997 steps in winter-rain Tasmania and south-west WA but only a weak across-catchment relation in SE-AU.
It found that the persistent deficit belonged to southern Australia after 1997; our climate-only LSTM leaves 1997 steps in Tasmania and south-west WA and none in the north.
Its contrast with the central-Chile megadrought motivates our regional controls.
Its monthly model left the 1946-1956 surplus; our LSTM also leaves most of the 1951-1958 surplus.
Long-record context for the pre-1957 surplus and earlier deficits.
Its state view of Victorian catchments is compared with our trend-versus-step result.
Its slow pre-1997 drift in gauge-relative rain is a possible source of a slow drift in our climate-adjusted series.
It treated four wet Tasmanian catchments separately; we find a 1997 step beyond climate in 26 Tasmanian catchments.
LSTM rainfall-runoff modelling on CAMELS-AUS; our model setup is similar in inputs and loss.
Community review of explanations for Millennium Drought rainfall-runoff changes.
Peterson et al. 2021: watersheds may not recover from drought; the state-shift hypothesis we test.
